title: React Render Cycle and Component Lifecycle
description: Understand when and why React components re-render. Learn about the render phase, commit phase, reconciliation algorithm, and how React decides what to update in the DOM. Master the mental model of React's lifecycle to write more efficient components.

steps.title: Understand What Triggers a Render
steps.explanation:
React components re-render when their state or props change. This is fundamental. Every setState call schedules a re-render. When a parent re-renders, all its children re-render by default (unless optimized).

Three things trigger renders: (1) State changes via setState, (2) Parent component re-renders, (3) Context value changes. That's it. Changing a ref doesn't trigger renders. Calling a function doesn't trigger renders. Only these three things.

Understanding this is crucial for debugging. If your component isn't updating, check: did state change? If it's updating too much, check: is parent re-rendering unnecessarily? Is state changing when it shouldn't?
steps.task:
Create a demonstration of render triggers: 1. Add console.log('RenderCycle rendered') at the top of your component 2. Add state 'parentCount' starting at 0 3. Add a button 'Update Parent' that increments parentCount 4. Create a child component 'ChildComponent' OUTSIDE RenderCycle: - Takes no props - Logs 'ChildComponent rendered' at the top - Returns
I am a child component
5. Render ChildComponent in RenderCycle 6. Click the button - notice BOTH components log renders 7. Display parentCount in your JSX Open the browser console to see the render logs!
hints: Put console.log at the very top of your component function
Create ChildComponent as a separate function outside RenderCycle
ChildComponent needs its own console.log
Use <ChildComponent /> in your JSX (self-closing tag)
Check browser console - both should log when you click the button

steps.title: Render Phase vs Commit Phase
steps.explanation:
React's render process has two phases. Understanding this is key to understanding React's performance.

Render Phase: React calls your component function, gets the new JSX, and compares it to the previous render. This is pure computation - no DOM changes yet. React can interrupt this phase if needed.

Commit Phase: React applies the changes to the actual DOM. This is synchronous and can't be interrupted. Only the DIFFERENCES found in the render phase get applied - React doesn't rebuild the entire DOM.

This two-phase approach is why React is fast. Calling your component function is cheap. Updating the DOM is expensive. React minimizes DOM updates by computing differences first.
steps.task:
Demonstrate the two phases:

1. Add state 'renderCount' starting at 0
2. Add console.log('RENDER PHASE: Computing JSX, renderCount = ' + renderCount) at the top
3. Add useEffect with NO dependency array that logs 'COMMIT PHASE: DOM updated'
4. Add a second useEffect with [] that logs 'COMMIT PHASE: Initial mount only'
5. Add a button that increments renderCount
6. Display renderCount

Check console:
- First load: see both commit phase logs (mount) and one render phase log
- Click button: see render phase log and the first commit log (not the mount-only one)
hints: First console.log goes at the top of the component (render phase)
First useEffect has NO dependency array (runs after every render)
Second useEffect has [] (runs only on mount)
Each phase runs at a different time - observe the console order
Render phase always runs before commit phase

steps.title: React's Reconciliation Algorithm
steps.explanation:
Reconciliation is how React figures out what changed. When you return new JSX, React doesn't replace the entire DOM - it compares the new JSX tree to the old one and updates only what changed.

The algorithm is smart but follows rules: (1) Different element types cause full replacement (div to span = unmount old, mount new), (2) Same type = keep DOM node, update attributes, (3) Keys identify which items in lists are the same across renders.

This is why keys matter in lists! Without keys, React assumes list items are the same based on position. [A, B, C] to [B, C, A] without keys = React updates all three. WITH keys = React just moves them. Huge performance difference.
steps.task:
Demonstrate reconciliation:

1. Create state 'items' as an array: [{ id: 1, text: 'First' }, { id: 2, text: 'Second' }, { id: 3, text: 'Third' }]
2. Map over items to render each one:
   - Use key={item.id} (proper reconciliation)
   - Create an input for each item with defaultValue={item.text}
3. Add a 'Reverse Order' button that reverses the items array: setItems([...items].reverse())
4. Type in the inputs, then click Reverse
5. Notice: with proper keys, the input VALUES move with their items!
   (If you remove keys, the values stay in place while text moves - wrong!)
hints: useState with array of objects: [{ id: 1, text: 'First' }, ...]
Map with key: items.map(item => <div key={item.id}>...)
Each item should render an input with defaultValue={item.text}
Reverse: setItems([...items].reverse()) - spread to create new array
Try removing key to see the difference in behavior!

steps.title: Batching and Asynchronous Updates
steps.explanation:
React batches state updates for performance. Multiple setState calls in the same event handler get batched into one re-render. This prevents unnecessary renders.

In React 18+, batching happens automatically everywhere - event handlers, promises, setTimeout, native events. Before React 18, only event handlers were batched.

Critical insight: setState is asynchronous. Calling setState doesn't immediately update the state - it schedules an update. If you call setState then immediately read state, you'll see the old value. This is why updater functions exist: setCount(c => c + 1) uses the latest value.
steps.task:
Demonstrate batching and updater functions:

1. Add state 'batchCount' starting at 0
2. Add button 'Wrong: Add 3':
   - Calls setbatchCount(batchCount + 1) THREE times
   - Add console.log after each call
   - Notice: only increases by 1, not 3!
3. Add button 'Correct: Add 3':
   - Calls setBatchCount(c => c + 1) THREE times
   - Increases by 3 correctly
4. Add console.log('Component rendered, batchCount = ' + batchCount) at top
5. Display batchCount

Notice in console:
- Multiple setState calls = only ONE render (batching)
- Updater function uses latest value, direct value doesn't
hints: Create two separate button handlers
First button: setBatchCount(batchCount + 1) called three times
Second button: setBatchCount(c => c + 1) called three times
Console.log at the top shows you only render once per click
The wrong way only increases by 1 because batchCount is stale

steps.title: Preventing Unnecessary Renders
steps.explanation:
By default, when a component renders, all its children render too. This is usually fine, but for expensive components or deep trees, it can cause performance issues.

Optimization techniques: (1) React.memo wraps a component and prevents re-render if props haven't changed, (2) useMemo caches expensive calculations, (3) useCallback caches functions so they're stable references.

Critical: only optimize when you have a measured performance problem. Premature optimization adds complexity for no benefit. Profile first, then optimize. Most components are fast enough without optimization.
steps.task:
Demonstrate preventing unnecessary renders: 1. Import React at the top: import React, { useState } from 'react' 2. Create state 'parentState' starting at 0 3. Create state 'childProp' starting at 0 4. Create a child component 'ExpensiveChild' wrapped in React.memo: - Takes a prop 'value' - Logs 'ExpensiveChild rendered with value: ' + value - Returns
Child value: {value}
5. Add button 'Update Parent' that increments parentState (NOT childProp) 6. Add button 'Update Child Prop' that increments childProp 7. Render 8. Display both parentState and childProp Notice: clicking 'Update Parent' doesn't log ExpensiveChild render (memo works!)
hints: Import React: import React, { useState } from 'react'
Create ExpensiveChild outside your main component
Wrap it: const ExpensiveChild = React.memo(function ExpensiveChild({ value }) { ... })
Two buttons update different state variables
ExpensiveChild only logs when childProp changes, not when parentState changes
